method: Tempo is quarter-note beats per minute, so one beat lasts 60 / BPM seconds. Two curves are offered. With the curve linear in time the tempo changes by the same amount every second: the beats covered grow quadratically and the change lasts 120 x beats / (start + end) seconds, so the average tempo is the arithmetic mean of the two tempos. With the curve linear in beats the tempo changes by the same amount on every beat, so each beat lasts 60 / its own tempo and the change lasts 60 x beats x ln(end / start) / (end - start) seconds, which is the reciprocal of the logarithmic mean of the two tempos; the beat-linear ramp is always the longer of the two and both agree when the tempos are equal. The table reports the tempo and elapsed time at 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of the beats: on the beat-linear curve the elapsed time is the integral of 60 / (start + (end - start) n / beats) over the beats played, and on the time-linear curve it comes from the quadratic beat count n = (start x t + (end - start) x t^2 / (2T)) / 60 for a total T. Tempos are limited to 10 to 400 BPM and the span to 0.25 to 256 beats; input is read as text, so a decimal needs a dot. Every published figure is rounded to three decimals and the page formats it for display. The page calculates in the browser with no audio engine, upload, storage or network access, and it neither plays nor records a metronome.
